scene.testo: It is 6 AM on the International Space Station. Outside the window, the temperature is minus 250 degrees Fahrenheit in the shade. Inside, the crew is sipping coffee in T-shirts. There is no furnace on board. So where does the warmth come from?

Here is the part that should not make sense. That same station travels at 17,500 miles per hour, about 250 miles above Earth. In sunlight it can swing past +250 degrees Fahrenheit. Cold and hot, minutes apart, all day long.

Imagine you are floating in that station right now. Your hair drifts up. Your coffee comes in a pouch with a straw. You drift past a window, and beyond the glass is a vacuum colder than any freezer you have ever opened.

So here is the question. How do astronauts survive the cold of space without heaters? The surprising answer is that space is not really cold the way you think. And the real danger is almost the opposite of freezing.

First, a confession. Space has no temperature in the way air does. Cold is really about air molecules bumping into your skin. In a vacuum, almost nothing bumps into you. So there is almost nothing to carry heat away.

On Earth, a winter wind steals your heat fast. That is convection and conduction. Your body hands warmth to the air, and the air carries it off. In space, those two thieves are almost completely missing. Only one remains.

That last thief is radiation. Your body glows in infrared light and slowly sends its heat out into the dark. It works, but it is slow. This is why a person in space does not freeze solid in seconds, like movies show.

Now flip it around. The sun in orbit is not filtered by air. Sunlight hits the station with about 1,360 watts on every square meter, measured by NASA. That is brutally strong. Metal skin in the sun heats up fast.
scene.q: sun shining on space station solar

scene.testo: And here is the twist. The station circles Earth about every 90 minutes. That means about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every single day. Light, dark, light, dark. Each trip swings the outside temperature by hundreds of degrees.

Picture the station like a roast in an oven that keeps switching on and off every 45 minutes. If nothing managed that swing, metal would flex, seals would crack, and equipment would fail. Something has to smooth it out.

The first answer is wrapped around the outside. Thermal blankets. Multiple thin layers of reflective film, like a super fancy emergency blanket from a first aid kit. Gold and silver colored sheets bounce heat away or keep it in.

Why layers? Because in a vacuum, gaps between layers cannot carry heat by touch. Each reflective sheet blocks a little more radiation. Stack enough of them, and heat struggles to cross. A thin film becomes a powerful shield.

That crinkly gold foil you see on satellites is not decoration. It is the thermos of space. Same idea as the double wall in your coffee flask, only built from many layers of film and a perfect vacuum.

The second answer is the paint. Surfaces on the station use special coatings and white or shiny finishes to reflect sunlight. White reflects more heat than black. You know this already. A white car stays cooler in a summer parking lot.

But the real hero is not a blanket. It is a cooling loop. The station has liquid ammonia flowing through pipes outside, and water loops inside. Together they act like a radiator and a plumbing system, moving heat where it is needed.

Here is the surprise. The station is not struggling to stay warm. It is struggling to stay cool. Inside, computers, lights, pumps, and seven crew members all create heat. Every bit of it must be thrown away into space.

Remember, there is no air outside to carry that heat off. On Earth, a fan can blow your computer cool. In a vacuum, heat has nowhere to go, unless you build a way. That is the job of those big white radiator panels.

Those radiators glow in infrared and send the extra heat out into space. The loop collects warmth from inside, carries it out, and lets it escape. It is a heater and an air conditioner in one, and it never rests.
scene.q: space station exterior radiators solar arrays

scene.testo: Now think about that for a second. A crew of astronauts on the station can warm the place just by living there. A resting human gives off roughly 100 watts of heat. That is about like an old incandescent light bulb.

Add up everything on board, and the station produces tens of thousands of watts of heat. Electronics, motors, lights, people. It is less like a freezer and more like a crowded server room that must be constantly chilled.

Inside, the crew keeps the cabin around room temperature. NASA documents show the station is typically held in the low 70s degrees Fahrenheit. That is comfortable enough for a T-shirt and shorts, no jacket needed.

And the air matters, too. There is no wind in space, but fans are running all the time inside. Why? Because in weightlessness, warm air does not rise. Without gravity, hot air simply stays put around your body.

On Earth, a candle flame pulls warm air up and fresh air in. That is convection, and gravity runs it. Take away gravity, and a bubble of stale, hot air can build around your face, so fans keep the air moving.

Now let us step outside, because here is where it gets dangerous. A spacewalk can last about 6 to 7 hours, based on NASA records. The astronaut is wearing a suit, and that suit is basically a personal spacecraft.

Inside the suit, an astronaut wears a garment threaded with thin tubes of water. It is called a liquid cooling and ventilation garment. Cool water flows past the skin and carries sweat and body heat away.

Think of it as underwear made of a spider web of plumbing. Why is it needed? Because working in a bulky pressurized suit is hard labor. Muscles burn energy, and the body makes heat that has nowhere to go.
Outside the suit, the sun side can be scorching. The shadow side can be deadly cold. NASA describes the suit exposed to extremes that run from about minus 250 degrees to plus 250 degrees Fahrenheit.

So the suit has to be a fortress. Many layers of insulation, a reflective outer shell, and a sealed pressure bladder. Between the astronaut and the vacuum is a stack of fabric roughly the same count as a good winter coat.

Yet the coldest part of the body is often the same as on a ski slope. Fingers. Astronauts have said gloves are the hardest part of a spacewalk. Hands can grow cold or sore when touching shaded metal for long periods.

The gloves have small heaters built in. That is right, heaters, but just for fingertips. NASA has said that some suit gloves include heating to keep hands working when holding cold tools in the shade.

On a hot sun side, the suit does the opposite. It pushes heat out through a device called a sublimator. Water turns directly from ice into vapor in the vacuum, and that process carries heat away from the cooling loop.

That detail is astonishing. The suit cools itself by letting water boil away into space. Crews have even carried the earlier Apollo-era version of this idea all the way to the Moon, where the heat was real.

Speaking of the Moon, let us look at what Apollo crews faced. On the lunar surface, sunlit ground can reach about 250 degrees Fahrenheit, while shadowed areas drop far below zero. The suits had to handle that swing.

Apollo suits used water cooling, too. Astronauts wore a garment with tubes under the suit, like the modern design. A spacecraft carried the water supply, and a sublimator dumped the heat into the vacuum of space.

Now back to the station. What about the long nights? Crew members sleep in small sleeping compartments, with a bag fastened to the wall. They float in it. And yes, it can feel chilly, so some tuck into that bag fully.

That bag is not about warmth from heaters. It is about holding you in place. Without gravity, your arms would drift out and bump into things. Zipping up keeps limbs close, and that keeps body heat close, too.

Compare that with a camping trip on Earth. You stay warm with a thick bag, a pad under you, and maybe a fire. The station skips all of it. The whole building is the heater, kept in balance by pumps and radiators.

Here is a comparison you know. Your house has a thermostat and a furnace. The station has the same idea, but reversed. The thermostat tells the system how much heat to throw away, not how much to make.

The scale is huge. The station is about as long as a football field, including its end zones, roughly 357 feet across its main truss, according to NASA. That is a lot of metal soaking up and shedding heat.

And it must survive that environment for years. Many parts have been in orbit since the first module launched on November 20, 1998. More than two decades of sun and shadow, and the thermal system keeps going.

Cold, though, is not a danger only to people. Fuel lines, batteries, and wires must stay above freezing, too. Small electric heaters do exist on spacecraft for parts like valves and thrusters, switched on only where needed.

So the title of this video is a little tricky. The station has no big furnace for the crew. But yes, small heaters exist in gloves and hardware. The main system is about moving and rejecting heat, not making more.
scene.q: engineer inspecting satellite thermal vacuum chamber

scene.testo: Before launch, spacecraft are tested in giant vacuum chambers. Engineers bake them under lamps and chill them with liquid nitrogen, copying orbit. If anything cracks or sticks, they find it on the ground, not in space.

Now here is the most surprising detail. In space, the astronaut's biggest temperature problem is usually getting rid of heat. Your body is a tiny furnace, and in a vacuum, it has to shout its warmth into the dark.

So when people ask how astronauts survive the cold without heaters, the real answer is wonderfully backward. They survive by staying cool, using blankets, mirrors, water loops, and radiators. Space is not freezing them. It is the hardest place to cool down.
